lessonTitle: Allergy and Atopic Disease: Food Allergy, Eczema and Anaphylaxis

blocks.text: A 14-month-old is given a spoonful of scrambled egg for the first time. Within ten minutes her face is blotchy, her lips swell and she vomits twice. She is still alert and breathing quietly. Is this a stomach bug, a skin problem, or the first appearance of IgE-mediated food allergy, and what would change if her voice became hoarse?

blocks.markdown: **Atopy** is the tendency to produce IgE antibodies to common environmental or food antigens. It links eczema (atopic dermatitis), food allergy, allergic rhinitis and asthma, which often appear in sequence in the same child (the 'atopic march'). In this unit we cover three things: how IgE-mediated food allergy presents, how eczema is managed, and how adrenaline and an action plan are used for anaphylaxis.

blocks.title: IgE-mediated (immediate) food allergy
blocks.text: A reproducible, immune-mediated adverse reaction to a food in which allergen-specific IgE on mast cells and basophils triggers histamine and mediator release. Symptoms typically begin within minutes and usually within about two hours of exposure. This differs from non-IgE-mediated allergy, where symptoms are delayed (hours to days) and mainly gastrointestinal or cutaneous, and from food intolerance, which is non-immune.

blocks.markdown:
**Mechanism, then features.** After sensitisation, re-exposure cross-links IgE on mast cells. Mediators cause vasodilatation and increased vascular permeability (urticaria, angioedema, hypotension), smooth muscle contraction (wheeze, vomiting, colic) and mucosal oedema (laryngeal swelling, stridor). Common triggers in UK children include cows' milk, egg, peanut, tree nuts, sesame, fish, shellfish and wheat. Features by system:

- **Skin**: urticaria, flushing, angioedema (the commonest features).
- **Gastrointestinal**: vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhoea.
- **Respiratory**: wheeze, cough, hoarse voice, stridor, throat tightness.
- **Cardiovascular**: pallor, floppiness, tachycardia, hypotension, collapse.

blocks.title: Is it IgE-mediated food allergy?
blocks.prompt: A 3-year-old has hives and lip swelling 15 minutes after eating a mouthful of a sesame-seed bun. She has had a similar episode once before. Her parents ask whether to 'just give a bit more to build tolerance'. Reason through the diagnosis and advice.

steps.text: Timing: onset within minutes of ingestion points to an immediate, IgE-mediated mechanism rather than a delayed non-IgE or intolerance reaction.

Features: urticaria and angioedema are typical mast cell mediator effects; there are no airway or circulatory features recorded, so this is an allergic reaction without anaphylaxis at this point, but it can progress.

Reproducibility: a similar earlier episode after the same food strengthens the history; allergy is diagnosed from a convincing history supported by tests such as skin prick testing or specific IgE, not by tests alone.

Advice: do not deliberately re-expose at home. Avoid the suspected food, treat any reaction, and refer for specialist assessment; any supervised challenge or reintroduction is decided by an allergy team.

blocks.answer: Probable IgE-mediated sesame allergy: immediate onset, urticaria and angioedema, repeat episode. Avoid, refer for specialist testing, and give emergency guidance; no home re-challenge.

blocks.caption: IgE-mediated versus non-IgE-mediated food allergy
rows: Reflux, loose stools, blood in stool, worsening eczema, faltering growth
Largely history and supervised elimination then reintroduction

blocks.markdown: **Childhood eczema.** Atopic eczema is a chronic relapsing itchy inflammatory skin disease caused by a defective skin barrier plus immune dysregulation. In infants it often affects the face and extensor surfaces; in older children, the flexures (antecubital and popliteal fossae). Management is stepped and the foundation is **emollients**, used generously every day even when the skin looks clear. Flares are treated with **topical corticosteroids** matched to site and severity (mild potency for face and flexures, stronger for thick skin on the trunk and limbs, in line with current NICE and BNFc guidance). Soap substitutes replace soap. Triggers (irritants, overheating, known allergens) are identified and avoided. Specialist options for severe disease include topical calcineurin inhibitors, wet wraps and systemic treatment. Check doses, potencies and durations against current BNFc/NICE/local guidance.

blocks.title: Choosing the eczema step
blocks.prompt: A 7-year-old has dry skin all over, and red, weeping, itchy patches in both elbow flexures for four days. The skin is crusted with yellow areas. He has had no fever and is otherwise well. Outline the management steps.

steps.text: Baseline: continue regular emollients and soap substitutes on the whole body; this repairs the barrier and reduces flare frequency.

Active inflammation: a topical corticosteroid of appropriate potency for flexural skin applied to the inflamed patches only, stopping as the flare settles (check potency and duration against BNFc/NICE guidance).
Crusting and weeping suggest secondary bacterial infection (commonly Staphylococcus aureus), so consider a topical or oral antibacterial according to local guidance and swabs if needed.
Safety net: grouped punched-out blisters, fever and rapid worsening suggest eczema herpeticum, which needs urgent same-day assessment and antiviral treatment.

blocks.answer: Emollients for the whole skin, topical steroid to inflamed flexures, treat probable secondary bacterial infection per local guidance, and recognise eczema herpeticum as an emergency.

blocks.title: Adrenaline is the first-line drug in anaphylaxis
blocks.text: Anaphylaxis is a life-threatening airway, breathing or circulation problem, usually with skin changes, after allergen exposure. The first-line treatment is intramuscular adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh, given immediately; antihistamines and steroids are not substitutes and do not treat airway or circulatory compromise.

blocks.markdown: **Using adrenaline.** Adrenaline acts on alpha-1 receptors (vasoconstriction, less oedema), beta-1 (increased heart rate and contractility) and beta-2 (bronchodilation, reduced mediator release). The teaching calculation for the intramuscular dose uses the 1 mg/mL (1 in 1000) preparation at 0.01 mg/kg, which equals 0.01 mL/kg. In practice, UK resuscitation and BNFc guidance gives age-banded doses and auto-injector strengths; always check against current Resuscitation Council UK, BNFc and local guidance. If there is no improvement after about five minutes, a further intramuscular dose is given, and an ambulance must always be called.

blocks.caption: Teaching calculation for IM adrenaline; verify against current guidance before any real use.

blocks.title: Adrenaline dose arithmetic (teaching calculation)
blocks.prompt: A 16 kg child has wheeze, hoarse voice and collapse after a bee sting. Using 0.01 mg/kg and the 1 mg/mL preparation, calculate the dose and volume.

steps.text: Volume = dose divided by concentration (1 mg/mL)

Route and action: inject intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh, call an ambulance, lie the child flat (or in a position of comfort if breathing is difficult), and repeat after about five minutes if there is no improvement. Verify against current guidance.

blocks.answer: 0.16 mg, which is 0.16 mL of 1 mg/mL adrenaline, given IM (teaching calculation).

items: Written allergy action plan: names the allergen, lists mild and severe signs, and states what to do at each.
Prescribed adrenaline auto-injectors (two), carried at all times, with parents, school and carers trained to use them.
Clear instruction to call an emergency ambulance after any adrenaline use, even if the child improves, because of the risk of a biphasic reaction.
Medical identification, school health plan, and in-date devices checked regularly.
Avoidance advice, reading of food labels, and follow-up with an allergy service.

blocks.title: Do not delay adrenaline
blocks.text: Delayed adrenaline is associated with worse outcomes. Waiting to see whether antihistamines help, or because the child has no skin rash, is a common and dangerous error. Poorly controlled asthma is a recognised risk factor for fatal food-anaphylaxis.

points: IgE-mediated food allergy causes immediate-onset skin, gastrointestinal, respiratory and cardiovascular features, usually within minutes to about two hours.
Eczema management rests on regular emollients, with topical corticosteroids for flares and prompt recognition of infection and eczema herpeticum.
Anaphylaxis is treated with immediate intramuscular adrenaline, an ambulance call, and a written action plan with trained carers.

questions.stem: Which feature best suggests an IgE-mediated rather than a non-IgE-mediated reaction to cows' milk in an infant?

options.text: Facial urticaria and lip swelling within minutes of a feed
Loose stools that gradually worsen over several days
Faltering growth over months
Mild reflux that began at 2 weeks of age

questions.correctOptionText: Facial urticaria and lip swelling within minutes of a feed

distractorRationale.a: Correct: immediate skin features are typical of IgE-mediated allergy.
distractorRationale.b: Delayed gastrointestinal symptoms over days fit non-IgE-mediated allergy.
distractorRationale.c: Faltering growth is a feature of chronic non-IgE-mediated disease or other conditions.
distractorRationale.d: Mild reflux from early infancy is common and not specific for IgE allergy.

questions.explanation: IgE-mediated reactions occur within minutes to about two hours because pre-formed IgE on mast cells releases mediators on re-exposure. Urticaria and angioedema are therefore the classic immediate features, whereas delayed or chronic gut symptoms point to non-IgE mechanisms.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old with known peanut allergy eats a biscuit at a party and within 10 minutes develops widespread hives, a hoarse voice and audible wheeze. What is the most appropriate immediate drug treatment?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh
Oral antihistamine and observe for 30 minutes
Oral prednisolone
Nebulised salbutamol alone

questions.correctOptionText: Intramuscular adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh

distractorRationale.a: Correct: airway and breathing features after allergen exposure define anaphylaxis, which needs IM adrenaline.
distractorRationale.b: Antihistamines relieve urticaria but do not treat airway or circulatory compromise and delay adrenaline.
distractorRationale.c: Steroids act too slowly to treat acute anaphylaxis.
distractorRationale.d: Salbutamol addresses bronchospasm only and does not treat laryngeal oedema or hypotension.

questions.explanation: Hoarse voice and wheeze after a known allergen mean airway and breathing involvement, so this is anaphylaxis. Intramuscular adrenaline is the first-line treatment, and an ambulance should also be called.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with eczema has had dry skin for months. Which approach is the foundation of management between flares?

options.text: Regular generous emollients and soap substitutes
Daily potent topical corticosteroid over the whole body
Routine oral antibiotics
Strict elimination of milk, egg and wheat from the diet

questions.correctOptionText: Regular generous emollients and soap substitutes

distractorRationale.a: Correct: emollients repair the barrier and reduce flares.
distractorRationale.b: Topical steroids are for flares, matched to site and severity, not continuous whole-body use.
distractorRationale.c: Antibiotics are for clinically infected eczema, not routine.
distractorRationale.d: Empirical food exclusion without a suggestive history is not recommended and risks nutritional harm.

questions.explanation: Eczema reflects a defective skin barrier, so leave-on emollients used daily are the basis of care. Steroids and antibiotics are added for inflammation and infection respectively, and diets are restricted only when a clear food trigger is identified.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old with eczema develops, over 24 hours, fever, malaise and clusters of uniform punched-out blisters with crusting on the cheeks and neck over previously inflamed skin. What is the most important action?

options.text: Urgent same-day assessment for eczema herpeticum with antiviral treatment
Increase the potency of the topical steroid
Reassure and continue emollients only
Start a food elimination diet

questions.correctOptionText: Urgent same-day assessment for eczema herpeticum with antiviral treatment

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this picture suggests herpes simplex superinfection, which needs urgent antiviral treatment.
distractorRationale.c: Reassurance misses a potentially serious complication.
distractorRationale.d: A dietary change is irrelevant to an acute infective picture.

questions.explanation: Fever with monomorphic punched-out vesicles on eczematous skin is the classic presentation of eczema herpeticum. It can spread and threaten the eyes and systemic health, so urgent antiviral therapy under current guidance is needed and topical steroids on affected areas should be reviewed.

questions.stem: Which statement about an allergy action plan is correct?

options.text: It should be shared with school and carers, who should know how to use the auto-injector
It is only needed once the child has had anaphylaxis twice
It makes calling an ambulance unnecessary after adrenaline
It replaces the need for allergen avoidance

questions.correctOptionText: It should be shared with school and carers, who should know how to use the auto-injector

distractorRationale.a: Correct: anyone caring for the child must recognise a reaction and act.
distractorRationale.b: A plan is indicated for any child at risk of severe reaction.
distractorRationale.c: An ambulance is still needed after adrenaline because of possible biphasic reactions.
distractorRationale.d: The plan supports, and does not replace, avoidance.

questions.explanation: Reactions often occur away from parents, so teachers and carers need written instructions and training. Even after successful adrenaline, emergency services must attend because symptoms can return.

questions.stem: A 22 kg child is in anaphylaxis. As a teaching calculation using 0.01 mg/kg of adrenaline, what intramuscular dose in mg is calculated? (Check real doses against current BNFc/Resuscitation Council UK guidance.)
questions.explanation: Dose equals 0.01 mg/kg multiplied by 22 kg, which gives 0.22 mg. This is a weight-based teaching calculation only; real prescribing follows age-banded guidance and the available device strengths.

questions.stem: A 12 kg toddler needs the weight-based teaching dose of 0.01 mg/kg adrenaline. Using the 1 mg/mL preparation, what volume in mL is drawn up? (Teaching calculation; verify against current guidance.)
questions.explanation: The dose is 0.01 x 12 = 0.12 mg. Because the concentration is 1 mg/mL, the volume in mL is numerically equal to the dose in mg, so 0.12 mL.

questions.stem: A mother brings her 9-month-old, who developed facial hives and two episodes of vomiting within 20 minutes of first trying peanut puffs. Describe how you would decide whether this is IgE-mediated food allergy and outline the advice you give the family.
markingGuide: Timing within minutes to about 2 hours suggests IgE-mediated mechanism
Features: urticaria, angioedema, vomiting; ask about wheeze, stridor, pallor, floppiness
History of exposure and reproducibility; other atopy such as eczema
Diagnosis rests on history supported by skin prick or specific IgE testing, interpreted by specialists
Avoid the suspected food and refer to allergy service; no home re-challenge
Teach recognition of severe features and when to call an ambulance
questions.explanation: Allergy is a clinical diagnosis: a convincing immediate-onset history is the starting point and tests support it. Given the risk of progression, families need clear avoidance and emergency advice with specialist referral rather than home re-exposure.

questions.stem: Explain why topical corticosteroids and emollients play different roles in childhood eczema, and describe two features that should make you suspect infection complicating eczema.
markingGuide: Emollients repair and protect the skin barrier and are used daily, even when skin is clear
Topical steroids reduce inflammation during flares, with potency matched to site and severity
Steroids applied to affected areas and stopped as flare settles, following BNFc/NICE guidance
Bacterial infection: crusting, weeping, yellow exudate, pustules, failure to respond to treatment
Herpes infection (eczema herpeticum): fever, clustered punched-out blisters, rapid spread, needs urgent antivirals
questions.explanation: Emollients treat the underlying barrier defect continuously, while steroids suppress active inflammation for limited periods. Recognising secondary bacterial or herpetic infection prevents treatment failure and serious complications.

questions.stem: A school nurse asks what a child's allergy action plan should contain and what happens after adrenaline is given. Outline your answer.
markingGuide: Identifies the allergen and the child's details and weight or device
Lists mild-moderate versus severe airway, breathing, circulation signs
States IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh first for anaphylaxis, with a repeat after about 5 minutes if no improvement
Calls an emergency ambulance; lie child flat unless breathing difficulty
Two in-date auto-injectors carried; staff trained
Hospital observation after adrenaline because of biphasic reactions
questions.explanation: A plan turns recognition into immediate action by carers, who are usually the first responders. Emergency attendance after adrenaline is essential since symptoms may recur after the drug wears off.
